'''John David Linsley''' (12 March 1925 – 15 September 2002) was an American physicist who performed pioneering research on [[cosmic ray]]s, particularly [[ultra-high-energy cosmic ray]]s. He did his most significant work from 1959 to 1978 using a ground-based array of detectors at Volcano Ranch in New Mexico. He is best known for being the first to detect an [[Air shower (physics)|air shower]] created by a primary particle with an energy of 10<sup>20</sup> eV.<ref name="Linsley Evidence">
{{cite journal
 | author = J. Linsley
 | year = 1963
 | title = Evidence for a Primary Cosmic-Ray Particle with Energy 10<sup>20</sup> eV
 | journal = [[Physical Review Letters]]
 | volume = 10 | pages = 146–148
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.10.146
| bibcode=1963PhRvL..10..146L
 | issue = 4
}}</ref><ref name="Fermilab"/> This was the highest energy cosmic ray observed up to that point. Linsley's observations suggested that not all cosmic rays are confined within the galaxy and showed the first evidence of a flattening of the cosmic ray spectrum at energies above 10<sup>18</sup> eV.<ref name="Fermilab">{{cite web |url = http://history.fnal.gov/findingaids/Linsley_ibatf2012001.html#d0e108/ |title = Finding Aid to the John Linsley Papers |publisher = Fermilab History and Archives Project, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory |date = 2012 |accessdate= 30 August 2012 }}</ref>

==Early life and career==

John David Linsley was born on March 12, 1925, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. His father, James Adolphus Linsley, was born in [[Morris, Minnesota]], and worked for the Minneapolis Transit Company as a streetcar conductor. His mother, Martha Carolina Linsley, was born in Follinge, Sweden, and was a graduate of the [[University of Minnesota]]. He had one sister, Ruth Anne Linsley Forman.<ref name="Fermilab"/><ref name="Dear Daddy">{{cite web |url=http://www.deardaddy.com/press/family_biographies.php |title=Linsley Family Biographies |accessdate=30 August 2012}}</ref>

Linsley was homeschooled by his mother for much of his childhood and graduated from [[Roosevelt High School (Minneapolis)|Roosevelt High School]] in Minneapolis in 1941. He attended the [[University of Minnesota]], graduating in 1946. While working on his bachelor's degree, Linsley also served in the U.S. Army from 1944 to 1946.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

After completing his undergraduate education, Linsley remained at the [[University of Minnesota]] to work on his Ph.D. under the direction of [[Edward P. Ney]].<ref>{{cite web |url = http://inspirehep.net/record/1046330/ |title = HEPNames Profile: John Linsley |publisher = INSPIRE |accessdate= 31 August 2012 }}</ref> He completed his Ph.D. in 1952, after which he worked as a research fellow at the [[University of Minnesota]] from 1952 to 1954. In 1954, Linsley took a job as a research associate at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). He held this position from 1954 to 1955 and from 1958 to 1972. While at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], Linsley was a member of a team led by [[Bruno Rossi]]. This team used an air shower array at [[Harvard University]]'s Agassiz Astronomical Station to observe air showers created by cosmic rays using ground-based liquid scintillator detectors. The analysis techniques Rossi's group developed laid the groundwork for the analysis of data from future arrays.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

==Volcano Ranch==

In 1957, [[Bruno Rossi|Rossi]] asked Linsley to design a much larger array based on the principles of the Agassiz array. Linsley worked with Livio Scarsi from the University of Milan to build an array of nineteen plastic scintillation detectors at [[Volcano Ranch experiment|Volcano Ranch]] near [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]]. They began making observations in the summer of 1959. On February 22, 1962, Linsley observed an air shower created by a primary particle with an energy greater than 10<sup>20</sup> eV, the highest energy cosmic ray particle ever detected at the time. Linsley's observations at Volcano Ranch expanded the known cosmic ray energy spectrum, clarified the structure of [[Air shower (physics)|air showers]], and provided the first evidence on [[ultra-high-energy cosmic ray]] composition and arrival directions. Linsley’s observations also indicated that not all cosmic rays are confined within the galaxy and provided the first evidence of a flattening of the cosmic ray spectrum at energies above 10<sup>18</sup> eV.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

Volcano Ranch was transferred from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] to the [[University of New Mexico]] in 1972 and Linsley took a position as adjunct professor of physics at the [[University of New Mexico]]. In 1973, Linsley created a denser array at Volcano Ranch to study the lateral distribution of [[Air shower (physics)|air showers]]. His work led him to develop the elongation rate theorem, which describes the rate of the change of the atmospheric depth of the air shower maximum with the energy of the primary particle.<ref>
{{cite journal
 | author = J. Linsley
 | year = 1977
 | journal = Proceedings of the 15th ICRC (Plovdiv 1977)
 | title = Untitled
}}</ref> In 1976, Linsley became a Research Professor of Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of New Mexico]]. Volcano Ranch was closed in 1978, when funding for the project ran out.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

==Later career==

After the closing of Volcano Ranch, Linsley continued his work in the field of cosmic rays. In 1979, he proposed detecting the fluorescence created by cosmic rays in the atmosphere through the use of a space-based observatory, a project which he called SOCRAS (Satellite Observation of Cosmic Ray Air Showers). This was the first proposal of a space-based cosmic ray observatory. He served as principal investigator on two research projects and collaborated on several others.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

Linsley was nominated for the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] by [[Pierre Victor Auger|Pierre Auger]] in 1980 for his work with cosmic rays. He won the Premio Internazionale San Valentino d’Oro in astrophysics in 1982. In 1986, he became a visiting professor at the [[University of Palermo]] and a senior fellow at the Istituto di Fisica Cosmica in [[Palermo]], Italy. In the mid-1990s, Linsley's idea of a space-based observatory was revived by the establishment of the international AirWatch consortium. Linsley was actively involved in this project, which evolved into AirWatch-OWL, and in the [[Extreme Universe Space Observatory]], another project to create a space-based observatory for the investigation of cosmic rays.<ref name="Fermilab"/>

John Linsley died on September 15, 2002, in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]]. He is survived by his son, Alessandro and his daughters, Mrs Joanna Linsley-Poe and Amina.
